item.title: Carney to brief cabinet, premiers on trade deal with the U.S.
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney is scheduled to brief his cabinet and Canada’s premiers today about the trade deal reached with the United States on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA -- Prime Minister Mark Carney is scheduled to brief his cabinet and Canada’s premiers today about the trade deal reached with the United States on Tuesday. Carney will chair a virtual cabinet meeting today and then hold a virtual meeting with premiers to discuss the deal that appears to have averted a new round of punishing tariffs on Canada. U.S. President Donald Trump paused for three days the latest tariff threat on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods pending the finalization of the deal. This is a breaking news update. CP’s earlier story follows below. WASHINGTON -- Prime Minister Mark Carney said a draft trade deal with the United States builds on Canada’s top bilateral trade terms and “reinforces that Canadian advantage.” In a statement posted on social media Wednesday — just hours after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a three-day pause on a new slate of tariffs on Canadian goods — Carney praised negotiators on both sides for hammering out an agreement. “We are now moving towards an agreement that reinforces that Canadian advantage, including by securing the best terms in each of Canada’s most important strategic sectors and providing greater certainty about our future trading relationship,” Carney said. Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said there was still work to finalize the deal, as he arrived for another meeting with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Washington. LeBlanc and Canada’s chief negotiator Janice Charette sat down with Greer Wednesday to continue working, after the terms of the deal they reached Tuesday were accepted by Trump. Shortly after 10 p.m. Tuesday, less than two hours before 50 per cent tariffs on a wide range of goods from Canada were set to take effect, Trump posted on Truth Social that a deal had been reached and the new tariffs were being paused for three days pending the finalization of the documents. For the first time since the latest high-stakes negotiations started last month, LeBlanc and Greer held a short, joint availability for reporters following their brief meeting Wednesday. LeBlanc and Charette have been back and forth to Washington since Trump announced the new tariffs in July, with the latest trip including multiple meetings since Aug. 10. Greer said he’s “happy with where we ended up” and now has to brief Congress and American stakeholders on what the two sides have been talking about. “We feel confident that we’ve reached an agreement that will not only continue to protect American workers, American jobs, American supply chains, but really strengthen the North American economy,” Greer said standing alongside LeBlanc outside the U.S. trade representative’s office. Greer added he expects it will make North America an energy and manufacturing “powerhouse.” The postponed round of tariffs would have hit $28 billion of Canadian goods, ranging from hockey sticks and ice skates to honey and some dairy products. Unlike previous tariffs Trump has imposed on Canada since his return to office in January 2025, these tariffs were not going to exempt any goods covered under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement, or CUSMA. Trump had threatened to impose those tariffs over Canada’s dairy supply management system, retaliatory tariff-free auto quotas and provincial bans on American alcohol in most provinces. A proclamation on the delay from The White House says Canada agreed to work toward resolving these trade irritants. Speaking to reporters outside the White House Wednesday, Trump said the deal would lift all of Canada’s tariffs on the U.S. but didn’t specify what exactly he was referring to. “It’s all subject to finalization,” he said. “I think it’s a very good deal for both parties.” He stressed the agreement would be good for American farmers and manufacturers. In a Truth Social post Tuesday, the president pointed to a revival of the Keystone XL pipeline as being part of the deal, followed by a fictional image of him appearing to yank a piece pipeline from the ground beside a grave marker that says ‘Buried by Biden.’ Former U.S. President Joe Biden revoked a key permit for the pipeline, which would have carried more oil from Alberta into the U.S. The new tariff deadline if the documents aren’t finalized is 12:01 a.m. ET Saturday. A spokesperson from the Dairy Farmers of Canada said in an emailed response that they are not commenting at this time due to a lack of concrete details. The spokesperson said the position of the dairy sector remains the same and they want to see commitments in the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement, known in Canada as CUSMA, upheld. The U.S. Trade Representative said on social media the deal will include comprehensive market access for all American goods, economic security commitments and digital trade alignment. LeBlanc would not give specifics but said supply management has been upheld. “The prime minister was very clear we needed to protect supply management, we needed to ensure that the supply management regime remained entirely intact, and I’m confident that that’s the case.” Carney said the government is “loyal” to the supply management system earlier this month. Dan Darby, Canadian Manufacturers and Exporters Association CEO, welcomed the tariff pause, but said uncertainty on the future of both the 50 per cent tariffs and earlier duties on steel, aluminum and autos continue to harm Canadian businesses. Darby is a member of the prime minister’s advisory council on Canada-U.S. relations, and said the council received a brief update Tuesday night. “There was an update just last night saying ‘talks continue, stay tuned. We’ll let you know,’” Darby said in a phone interview. Darby said any relief on the 50 per cent tariffs is a step in the right direction, but the manufacturing sector still needs to see movement on the steel and aluminum tariffs. Progress on those tariffs “will help take a bit of pressure off Canadian manufacturers and also perhaps provide some hope and some kind of stability,” Darby said. The industry association CEO said trade uncertainty is “the killer of any business.” “That’s the number 1 driver on why (Canadian manufacturers are) holding back on investment or holding back in hiring or even looking at other supply chains,” he said. Chris Swonger, president and CEO of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, said the organization appreciates Trump wanting to restore access for American spirits products across Canada. Several Canadian provinces pulled U.S. booze from store shelves last year after Trump imposed tariffs. The bans on U.S. liquor remain in place in all but Saskatchewan and Alberta. “These provincial bans have caused exports of American spirits to drop by more than 70 per cent, leaving American distillers caught in the middle of a broader trade dispute,” said Swonger in a statement. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party was relieved to hear there was a “new and excellent deal” in the works. “We hope that over the next couple of days we’ll hear the good news that Mr. Carney will have kept his promise and Canadians will get (an) even better deal than we had before,” he said at a press conference in Charlottetown. Poilievre added that deal should include zero tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber as well as an exemption to the “Buy America” policies. Trump returned to office set on changing Biden’s Keystone decision. Earlier this year, he signed an executive order for permits to revive parts of the project. It’s not clear how much of the trade talks between Canadian and American officials focused on the energy project. Carney spoke with Trump by phone Tuesday, hours before the U.S. was to bring in the punishing tariffs. Canadian officials were also looking to see relief on existing tariffs that target steel, aluminum, lumber and autos. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 19, 2026. — Written by David Baxter in Ottawa and Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington

Barry Schwartz, President & CIO, Baskin Wealth Management Focus: North American large caps

Top Picks: Costco , Alimentation Couche-Tard , Berkshire Hathaway MARKET OUTLOOK: Earnings are the only narrative we pay attention to as long-term investors, and we are very pleased with our portfolio holdings results so far for the second quarter (Q2). We continue to see many excellent values in our portfolio, given accelerating earnings growth with no corresponding stock price recovery. Over the past few years, this has been a one decision market, own the Nasdaq. We think returns will be more challenging going forward given that the market winners’ valuation reflects a lot of good news in the future. We are sticking with companies that can grow their earnings by at double digits over the next five years and we see lots of opportunities in dislocated high-quality North American equities. Costco (COST NASD) Costco continues to have strong comp growth partly from digital initiatives and is gaining market share especially in gas station amidst high fuel prices. We believe that Costco can grow its earnings per share at double digits for many years to come. Alimentation Couche-Tard (ATD TSX) Alimentation Couche-Tard benefitted from fuel price volatility this quarter from sophisticated fuel trading but is also seeing results from internal initiatives to add loyalty to its stores. It recently announced its largest ever deal, acquiring over 13,000 convenience stores in Poland and Romania. Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.B NYSE) After a slow start, we believe Berkshire CEO, Greg Abel is fast at work trying to allocate the hundreds of billions of cash. We are pleased to see that Berkshire stepped up its share buyback program as well as the company reported much better results for its operating businesses. item.title: Why is Trump talking about the Keystone XL pipeline?
item.description: Trump is talking about the project again five years after it was shut down by Biden when he was president. Here's everything you need to know.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. President Donald Trump hinted that he may revive an old pipeline project that would export oil from Canada to the U.S. as part of a pending trade deal. In a Truth Social post shared Tuesday night, Trump said he had suspended the 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods for three days , two hours before they were set to take place on Wednesday.

The deal, he stated, may include revitalizing the Keystone XL pipeline, a long hotly-contested project that has been in the works for almost a decade. Trump had attempted to revive the project during his first presidency as part of his then-campaign promises, but the pipeline was quashed by Joe Biden in the first year of his term. “The great Keystone XL Pipeline, long ago killed by Sleepy Joe Biden, may be awoken from the grave!” Trump’s social media post reads . He then published an AI-generated image of himself hoisting the Keystone XL pipeline out of a gravesite marked by a tombstone labelled “BURIED BY BIDEN.” Donald Trump tariffs on Canada Prime Minister Carney did not mention the pipeline in his own statement on Trump’s announcement. “Substantial progress has been made, although there is important work still to be done,” read the statement. First proposed in 2008, the project has seen a rocky journey, piled with legal barriers, opposition from environmental and Indigenous activists, and subject to the whims of U.S presidents at different points in time. What is Keystone XL? It has been proposed as an expansion project that would carry Canadian crude oil to the U.S. Gulf Coast and, if built, potentially increase those exports to the U.S. by more than 12 per cent. The current Keystone pipeline, first proposed in 2005 and built between 2008 and 2010, runs from Hardisty, Alta., across Saskatchewan and Manitoba and before crossing the U.S. near Haskett, Man., into North Dakota, Illinois and Nebraska . Keystone XL, if it had gone ahead, would have seen a direct route built between Hardisty and Steele City, Neb. However, only the U.S. portions of the extension have been constructed so far. Trump hinted at reviving the Keystone XL expansion project in his social media post on Tuesday night, five years after it was put to bed by Joe Biden. (The Associated Press) Trump hinted at reviving the Keystone XL expansion project in his social media post on Tuesday night, five years after it was put to bed by Joe Biden. (The Associated Press) How was it initially approved? The project was first proposed in 2008 by its then-owners TC Energy Corp. and ConocoPhilips. At the time, TC Energy Corp. was called TransCanada Corp. The Canadian Energy Board approved the project in 2010, but that came with 22 conditions on safety, environmental protection and landowner rights. Then-U.S. president Barack Obama was the first to shut it down two years later, in January 2012. Former U.S. President Barack Obama waves to the crowd following a speech before the Montreal Board of Trade Tuesday, June 6, 2017 in Montreal. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Paul Chiasson Former U.S. president Barack Obama waves to the crowd following a speech before the Montreal Board of Trade Tuesday, June 6, 2017, in Montreal. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Paul Chiasson Why is it so controversial? The project has seen major opposition from legislators and activists, citing environmental concerns, lack of legal oversight and unconstitutional use of state law to review the routes. Obama rejected the project in 2012 after U.S. legislators passed a bill in December 2011 that stated the president had to make a decision on the pipeline’s future in 60 days. Obama argued that this did not allow much time to review the new route but said TransCanada was free to submit another application. Between 2012 and 2016 , project costs ballooned as TransCanada looked to build southern legs of the expansion. While the company found favour in the Nebraska state government and a Republican-led U.S. Congress, the project was repeatedly shot down through legal challenges from pipeline opponents and a veto from the Obama administration. AM800-NEWS-DONALD-TRUMP-MICHIGAN-GETTY-1.2168036 Then-Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump addresses supporters during a campaign rally on Nov. 8, 2016, in Grand Rapids, Michigan. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images) Trump, in his 2016 presidential campaign, vowed to bring back the project if elected. In January 2017, he signed an executive order approving the project with plans to renegotiate the terms. The project still faced legal challenges over the next two years with construction getting underway in April 2020. In November, Biden was elected president and shut down the project on his first day of presidency. Why did Biden cancel the project? Biden cancelled the project in January 2021 , stating that it did not align with his administration ’s economic and environmental objectives. He had served as U.S. vice-president during the Obama administration. President Joe Biden speaks during a Department of Defense Commander in Chief farewell ceremony at Joint Base Myer-Henderson Hall, Jan. 16, 2025, in Arlington, Va. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci, File) U.S. President Joe Biden speaks during a Department of Defense Commander in Chief farewell ceremony at Joint Base Myer-Henderson Hall, Jan. 16, 2025, in Arlington, Va. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci, File) Then-Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau expressed disappointment over the cancellation and stated that his representatives were pressing the Biden administration to reconsider. Then-Alberta premier Jason Kenney threatened legal action if the project was scrapped. What has happened since? The project remained buried until Trump entered his second term as president. In February 2025, Trump posted on social media that he wanted to revive the Keystone XL project. In October, Carney pitched the project to Trump in exchange for relief from U.S. steel and aluminum tariffs on Canada’s industries, to which Trump was “very receptive,” according to media reports published then . In March, Alberta Liberal MP Corey Hogan confirmed that the pipeline was being used as leverage in trade talks with the U.S. “As we start thinking about some of the exposed industries and some of those that are really being hit hard by tariffs, we’ve got to have things to negotiate with, and energy is one of those things,” Hogan told CTV’s Power Play at the time. He added it would be “foolish” for the federal government not to “think about the opportunities” the pipeline project could provide. While the pipeline did not appear to be part of the pending trade deal, it could become a “sticking point” for Trump, according to CTV News political analyst Eric Ham. He told CTV News Channel on Wednesday that the situation seems “mysterious,” but noted Trump has prioritized “oil and energy” as a key component in his administration and in negotiations with Canada and other countries. “We saw how the president was willing to invade, frankly, Venezuela over energy,” Ham said. “So this has always been a priority.” Related Stories Industry experts see ‘steep barriers’ to Keystone XL revival Opens in new window Keystone XL ‘one of the cards’ Canada has in U.S. trade negotiations: Liberal MP Opens in new window
